content.text: Never training on the test set isn't enough. Every time you keep a model, a setting or a feature because it scored best on the test set, that set has helped build your model, and its score drifts upward. Make every choice on a validation set or with cross-validation, and score the test set once, at the end.

A team spends two weeks on a churn model. Every afternoon someone tries a few new settings, checks accuracy on the held-out test set and keeps the winner. The model never trains on a single test row, so the final number goes into the launch deck with confidence. A month after launch, live accuracy is lower than promised and nobody can find a bug. There isn't one. The evaluation was the problem.
The common misconception
Many developers believe the test set stays clean as long as the model never trains on it, so using it to compare models and tune settings is fine. It's an easy belief to hold:

items.text: The first rule everyone learns is "don't train on the test set", and this workflow follows it to the letter:
Reading a score feels read-only. Nothing about the model changes when you print its test accuracy.
Keeping the best-scoring candidate sounds like common sense, and on a small dataset a third split feels like wasted data.

content.text: The half-truth: the model's weights never saw the test rows. But you did, and you made decisions based on them. scikit-learn's guide to common pitfalls puts it plainly: test data should never be used to make choices about the model.
What actually happens
Training doesn't end when
fit
returns. Choosing a tree depth, a feature set, a preprocessing step or a model family are decisions too, and they're learned from whatever data you judge them on.
Choosing is part of training

scikit-learn's grid search guide describes model selection as a way of using labeled data to "train" the parameters of the grid. If the test set drives those choices, it's training data, just used more slowly. The cross-validation guide names the result: when settings are tweaked until the model performs best on the test set, knowledge about the test set can leak into the model, and the metrics no longer report how it will do on new data. It's a form of
data leakage
that never touches
fit
Picking the maximum picks the luck

Every test score is the model's real skill plus noise: which rows happened to land in the test set. Compare two candidates and the noise rarely matters. Compare 200 and keep the top one, and you also select the candidate whose noise was most flattering. The winner sits at the top of a noisy list, so its score is biased upward.

To see it beyond doubt, give the model nothing to learn. The script draws coin-flip labels, so no model can beat 50% on new data. It tries 200 decision-tree settings, keeps the one with the best test score, and checks it on 10,000 extra rows that stand in for production.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import ParameterGrid, train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.normal(size=(11_000, 20))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=11_000)  # coin-flip labels: nothing to learn
X, X_new, y, y_new = train_test_split(X, y, train_size=1000, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=200, random_state=0)

grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 11), "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10, 20, 40],
        "max_features": [2, 5, 10, 20]}  # 200 combinations
results = []
for params in ParameterGrid(grid):
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(**params, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    results.append((tree.score(X_te, y_te), tree))  # judged on the test set
score, best = max(results, key=lambda r: r[0])
print(f"test accuracy     {score:.3f}")
print(f"new data accuracy {best.score(X_new, y_new):.3f}")
# test accuracy     0.610
# new data accuracy 0.503

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import ParameterGrid, train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.normal(size=(11_000, 20))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=11_000)
X, X_new, y, y_new = train_test_split(X, y, train_size=1000, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=200, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X_tr, y_tr, test_size=200,
                                            random_state=0)  # 600 / 200 / 200
grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 11), "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10, 20, 40],
        "max_features": [2, 5, 10, 20]}
results = []
for params in ParameterGrid(grid):
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(**params, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    results.append((tree.score(X_val, y_val), tree))  # judged on validation
score, best = max(results, key=lambda r: r[0])
print(f"validation accuracy {score:.3f}")  # used to choose: optimistic
print(f"test accuracy       {best.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")  # looked at once
print(f"new data accuracy   {best.score(X_new, y_new):.3f}")
# validation accuracy 0.555
# test accuracy       0.505
# new data accuracy   0.498

content.text: The winner reports 0.610 on the test set and gets 0.503 on new data. Not one test row was used for training, yet the reported number is 11 points too high for a model that knows nothing. With real signal the same inflation is harder to spot: the model is genuinely good, just not as good as the test set claims.
The fix adds one split. Carve a
validation set

out of the training data and make every choice there. The validation winner is just as lucky, 0.555, because it was picked the same way. But the test set played no part in the choice, so its score, 0.505, tracks the 0.498 on new data.
Three sets, three jobs
Google's Machine Learning Crash Course divides the data three ways, each with one job:

items.text: : the model learns its weights from it.
on it, as often as you like.
: you confirm the final choice on it, at the end.

content.text: The Crash Course also warns that test and validation sets "wear out" with repeated use: the more you consult them, the more the model fits their quirks and the less you can trust them about new data. Its remedy is to refresh them with newly collected data when you can.
Cross-validation replaces the validation set, not the test set
On a small dataset, one validation split is noisy and costs rows.
Cross-validation

uses the training data better by rotating which part plays validation. The scikit-learn guide is precise about its scope: with cross-validation the validation set is no longer needed, but a test set should still be held out for final evaluation. The grid search guide says the same for
GridSearchCV
: run the search on a development set and compute the final metrics on a separate evaluation set it never saw.

The score you picked the winner by is honest
It's optimistic too: 0.555 on validation for a model stuck at 0.5
Cross-validation removes the need for a test set

A test set stays trustworthy forever

blocks.title: Treat the test run as a release step

content.text: Put the final evaluation in its own script that runs once per release, and record the score with the date and the model version. If someone wants to rerun it "just to check" after changing something, the test set is becoming a validation set. Size it for the precision you need, too: at 50% accuracy on 200 rows, one standard error is about 3.5 points.

Any decision you make by looking at test results leaks: which features to keep, which preprocessing to use, which model family wins, when to stop training, where to put the decision threshold. The leak is the same whether you automate the choice in a loop or make it by eye in a notebook.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Split off the test set first

content.text: Hold it out before you explore, plot or tune. The Crash Course also says to delete test examples that duplicate training examples: the only fair test is on new examples.

items.title: Make every choice on validation data

content.text: Use a validation split, or cross-validation on the training part, for hyperparameters, features, preprocessing and thresholds.
Fix the whole pipeline and its settings, then score the test set and report that number, not the validation score.
If the test score disappoints, go back to work, but the old test set is now a validation set. Judge the next version on fresh data.
Keep a record of each test evaluation, so the team knows how worn the test set is.
Key takeaways

items.text: Never training on the test set isn't enough: never choose by it either.
Keeping the best of many candidates inflates its score; a coin-flip model reported 0.610 and got 0.503 on new data.
Learn on the training set, choose on validation data or cross-validation, and confirm on the test set once.
Cross-validation replaces the validation set, not the test set, and a test set you keep reusing wears out.
